claim: Working memory (WM) is one of the most affected cognitive domains in multiple sclerosis (MS).
source: Working memory (WM) is one of the most affected cognitive domains in multiple sclerosis (MS), which is mainly studied by the previously established binary model for information storage (slot model).
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Continuous reproduction paradigms allow for assessing the distribution of error in recalling information, providing new insights into the organization of the WM system.
source: Moreover, continuous reproduction paradigms allow for assessing the distribution of error in recalling information, providing new insights into the organization of the WM system.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about continuous reproduction paradigms and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The study demonstrated an overall increase in recall error in MS.
source: Our results demonstrated an overall increase in recall error and decreased recall precision in MS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the Results section and Figure 2.

claim: The study demonstrated decreased recall precision in MS.
source: Our results demonstrated an overall increase in recall error and decreased recall precision in MS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the Results section and Figure 2.

claim: Sequential paradigms were better in distinguishing healthy control from relapsing-remitting MS.
source: While sequential paradigms were better in distinguishing healthy control from relapsing-remitting MS, MGL were more accurate in discriminating MS subtypes (relapsing-remitting from secondary progressive), providing evidence about the underlying mechanisms of WM deficit in progressive states of the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis data presented in Figure 4.

claim: MGL were more accurate in discriminating MS subtypes (relapsing-remitting from secondary progressive).
source: While sequential paradigms were better in distinguishing healthy control from relapsing-remitting MS, MGL were more accurate in discriminating MS subtypes (relapsing-remitting from secondary progressive), providing evidence about the underlying mechanisms of WM deficit in progressive states of the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Imprecision in decoding information was responsible for WM dysfunction in MS.
source: Furthermore, computational modeling of the results from the sequential paradigm determined that imprecision in decoding information and swap error (mistakenly reporting the feature of other presented items) was responsible for WM dysfunction in MS.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 3.

claim: Swap error (mistakenly reporting the feature of other presented items) was responsible for WM dysfunction in MS.
source: Furthermore, computational modeling of the results from the sequential paradigm determined that imprecision in decoding information and swap error (mistakenly reporting the feature of other presented items) was responsible for WM dysfunction in MS.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 3.

claim: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating inflammatory disorder characterized by demyelinating central nervous system (CNS) plaques creating a progressive neurodegenerative state with heterogeneous clinical characteristics.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating inflammatory disorder characterized by demyelinating central nervous system (CNS) plaques creating a progressive neurodegenerative state with heterogeneous clinical characteristics (Benedict et al., 2020; Dobson and Giovannoni, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Benedict et al., 2020 and Dobson and Giovannoni, 2019.

claim: Impairment in cognitive function is a common clinical manifestation of MS.
source: Impairment in cognitive function is a common clinical manifestation of MS, which detrimentally affects different aspects of patients' daily life, from decreased physical performance and productivity to unemployment (Benedict et al., 2020; Clemens and Langdon, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Benedict et al., 2020 and Clemens and Langdon, 2018.

claim: One of the frequently affected domains of cognition in MS is working memory (WM).
source: One of the frequently affected domains of cognition in MS is working memory (WM) (Vacchi et al., 2017), which, due to its essential role in several cognitive processes (Miller et al., 2018; Nee and D'Esposito, 2016), is one of the main areas of MS research (Costers et al., 2021; Covey et al., 2011; Hulst et al., 2017; Rocca et al., 2014; Vacchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations including Vacchi et al., 2017.

claim: The slot model of WM considers WM as a short-term storage for a limited number of items.
source: In this quantized model, WM is considered a short-term storage for a limited number of items (Cowan, 2001; Ma et al., 2014; Miller, 1956), storing the information in a binary format.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cowan, 2001; Ma et al., 2014; and Miller, 1956.

claim: Recent observations from analog recall paradigms determined dynamic allocation of WM resources.
source: Nonetheless, recent observations from analog recall paradigms assessing the precision of WM determined dynamic allocation of WM resources (Bays et al., 2009; Bays and Husain, 2008; Gorgoraptis et al., 2011; Schneegans and Bays, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bays et al., 2009; Bays and Husain, 2008; Gorgoraptis et al., 2011; and Schneegans and Bays, 2016.

claim: There are three different sources of error for recalling information in visual WM tasks with connected features: Gaussian variability in response around the target value, Gaussian variability in response around the non-target value (swap error), and random responses.
source: According to the study of Bays et al., there are three different sources of error for recalling information in visual WM tasks with connected features (Bays et al., 2009). They are identified as (i) the Gaussian variability in response around the target value (target response proportion), (ii) Gaussian variability in response around the non-target value, that is, mistakenly reporting feature of other presented items (swap error), and (iii) random responses (uniform response proportion) (Bays et al., 2009; Zokaei et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bays et al., 2009 and Zokaei et al., 2020.

claim: Random response contributes to the impairment of visual WM in Parkinson's disease.
source: It was determined that random response and swap error contribute to the impairment of visual WM in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases, respectively (Liang et al., 2016; Zokaei et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2016 and Zokaei et al., 2020.

claim: Swap error contributes to the impairment of visual WM in Alzheimer's disease.
source: It was determined that random response and swap error contribute to the impairment of visual WM in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases, respectively (Liang et al., 2016; Zokaei et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2016 and Zokaei et al., 2020.
